idiom_name: mapper class per aggregate wrapping sqlite3_stmt / PGresult in RAII wrappers
implementation_notes: The mainstream C++ answer is still a hand-written mapper: a class per aggregate that owns the connection handle plus RAII wrappers around sqlite3_stmt or libpq results, with find/update methods that bind parameters and build the domain object field by field. std::optional, std::variant and range-based iteration make the translation readable; the domain class itself needs no annotations and no library include. Keep the prepared statements in the mapper (or a statement cache) so the pattern also buys statement reuse.
pitfalls: Wrapping every statement in RAII is not optional: an exception thrown between prepare and finalize leaks the statement and pins the connection's resources.
sqlite3_column_text returns a pointer valid only until the next step/finalize; copy into std::string inside the mapper or return dangling data.
Hand-written mappers drift from the schema silently - a column added to the table but not to the mapper leaves a default-constructed field.

variants.name: ODB compiler-generated mapping from #pragma db declarations
variants.idiom_name: ODB #pragma db object/member declarations in a separate header
variants.implementation_notes: ODB moves the mapper into a code generator: the compiler reads #pragma db declarations plus a database profile and emits the persistence classes (load, update, erase, query) for your own types. The pragmas can be kept out of the domain header entirely - a separate *-odb.hxx carries them - which makes the mapping non-intrusive in the literal sense; the generated odb::database is the session and odb::transaction is the unit of work. Choose it when the schema is large and predictable and a build-time dependency on the ODB compiler is acceptable.
pitfalls: The generated code is a build dependency: schema or pragma changes require regeneration, so the ODB compiler becomes part of the toolchain and CI image.

Member pragmas still reference members of the domain type, so a renamed or hidden field is a compile error at generation time rather than at mapper level - keep the *-odb.hxx next to the mapper, never in the domain header.
Generated mappers assume the default constructor; classes without one need explicit factory/ctor pragmas.

variants.name: sqlite_orm declarative storage bindings (header-only)
variants.implementation_notes: sqlite_orm is a header-only ORM whose mapping is declared rather than coded: make_storage names the database, make_table the table, and make_column binds each column to a pointer-to-member of the domain struct, so the struct itself stays untouched. get/update/insert on the storage are the mapper operations and the library forms the SQL. It is the pragmatic C++ choice when the store is SQLite and the team wants schema and type checking without a code generator.
variants.code_sketch:
struct Customer { long id; std::string name; };        // untouched domain type

auto storage = make_storage("app.sqlite",
    make_table("customers",
        make_column("id",   &Customer::id, primary_key()),
        make_column("name", &Customer::name)));          // declarative mapper definition

auto c  = storage.get<Customer>(42);                     // load
c.name  = "Ada";
storage.update(c);                                       // save
pitfalls: The storage definition is the mapper: a renamed member fails to compile (good), but a reordered make_column list silently changes the SQL binding order.
It is an SQLite-only mapper, so the layer cannot be reused if the application later moves to a server database - that step means rewriting the mappers.
Embedded SQLite allows one writer at a time; concurrent writes need WAL plus a busy timeout or a serialised access policy in the mapper.
